problems.source_says: c246 (Chen, Huang, Han, Zhang, Lou, Zhong 2026, Australasian Journal of Educational Technology 42(4), 165-185, doi 10.14742/ajet.11512) analyzes the same 62 students. It matches c041 on every sample detail: 62 students, 41 female (21 male, the 33.9% in c041), ages 18 to 27 (M = 22.58, SD = 2.53), N = 31 per sequence, ChatGPT-4 versus Mr. Ranedeer, a Product Improvement Task on a stuffed bunny and a portable coffee maker, 17 (SD 7) and 20 (SD 6) minutes per condition, rater reliabilities 0.88, 0.90, and 0.86, self-efficacy alphas 0.89 and 0.88, and the same means, SDs, and p-values for quality, elaboration, and originality. Neither paper cites the other. Under codebook Sections 2 and 8 the two papers share one sample_id, and only one primary record per sample, question, and comparison type can enter a pooled estimate, so these 62 people count once.
problems.quote: A total of 62 Chinese university students (41 female) from a normal university participated in the study.

Full text: https://ajet.org.au/index.php/AJET/article/download/11512/2322. Compare c041 PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 3.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 and Fig. 2; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1.

problems.source_says: c041 alone supports null: it calls the design counterbalanced and never says random. But c246, which reports the same 62 students, labels the allocation step 'Random assignment of feedback sequence' and puts N = 31 under each sequence. On that evidence 62 people were randomized to an order (31 and 31), and all 62 were analyzed. The text of c246, like that of c041, says only that 'A counterbalanced design was implemented', so the random assignment rests on the figure. This also bears on criterion 1 and on the form's first open question.
problems.locator: c246 PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Figure 3 (The experimental procedure); c246 PDF p. 8 (printed p. 172), Procedure. Compare c041 PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 and Fig. 2.

problems.source_says: c246 reports the same Wilcoxon tests on the same 62 people: z = -3.24, r = -0.41 (quality), z = -6.25, r = -0.79 (elaboration), and z = -1.65, r = -0.21 (originality). There r = |z|/sqrt(62) holds for all three, and z = -1.65 gives the printed p = .098. In c041, the elaboration r = .62 implies z = 4.88 at N = 62, not 6.25, and the originality r = .18 implies p = .156, not .098. This answers the form's open question on the originality r and p, and it shows that the elaboration r is also wrong. A standard error should come from the c246 z values, not from the c041 r values.
problems.quote: elaboration (p < .001, r = -0.79). For originality, no statistically significant difference was found between conditions (p = 0.098, r = -0.21).

confirmed.statement: c041 reports 62 students: 32 undergraduates and 30 graduate students, 33.9% male (21 of 62). The abstract says each of the 62 did both tasks.
confirmed.locator: c041 PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 3.1; PDF p. 1 (printed p. 376), Abstract

confirmed.statement: Fig. 2 puts N = 31 in each order. 15 undergraduates and 16 graduates did the standard condition first, and 17 undergraduates and 14 graduates did the personalized condition first. The sums (32 and 30) match Sect. 3.1.
The counts are people. Every student used both tools, one per task, so each arm's n_analyzed of 62 counts the same 62 people, and the study total is 62, not 124.
confirmed.locator: c041 PDF p. 1 (printed p. 376), Abstract; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 and Fig. 2

confirmed.statement: c041 reports no exclusion, dropout, or missing data. I read all 13 pages, and the chapter has no appendix or supplement. The one exclusion it names is AOI 2, a screen area left out of the eye-tracking analysis, not a person.
confirmed.locator: c041 PDF pp. 1-13; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 382), Sect. 3.4.3

confirmed.statement: The eye-tracking tests used 62 people. r = |Z|/sqrt(62) reproduces every r in Table 1 (Z = -0.73, -0.31, -2.39 give .09, .04, .30), and the rounding allows only N = 62 to 65. This is derived, not printed.

The creative-performance tests used 62 people, not 186 solutions or 124 observations. c246 prints the same means, SDs, and p-values with z and r, and its r values equal |z|/sqrt(62), with rounding that allows only N = 62 or 63. With N = 186 the quality r would be .24, not .41.
c246 also reports no exclusions ('the final sample size of 62 participants'), and its regression df2 values (56 to 59) are consistent with 62 people in each model.
confirmed.locator: c246 PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169), Participants; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 176), Table 5

confirmed.statement: The who field matches Sect. 3.1: ages 18 to 27 (M = 22.6, SD = 2.5), social sciences, life sciences, and technical disciplines, almost all with prior GAI experience, more familiar with ChatGPT than with Mr. Ranedeer, and compensated.

participants.country = not_stated is faithful to c041, which never names the country. c246 says the same students were Chinese university students at a normal university, with materials in Chinese and ethics approval from Zhejiang Normal University, so the shared sample is in China.

confirmed.statement: Criterion 2 holds on S1 alone: 62 people analyzed across both arms, above 50. The overlap with c246 does not lower the count. It means the 62 people enter the atlas once.
confirmed.locator: c041 PDF p. 1 (printed p. 376), Abstract; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 3.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Fig. 2

summary: The people counts hold: 62 students did both conditions (31 per order in Fig. 2), neither c041 nor c246 reports an exclusion, and the printed Z and r values fit 62 people analyzed, so criterion 2 is met on S1. The coding is still refuted because sample_overlap is empty although c246 (AJET 2026) analyzes the same 62 students with the same creative-performance results, and the c246 Fig. 3 says the order was randomly assigned, so n_randomized can be 62 and criterion 1 needs another look.
